body.text: Attribution: Rajoli Siddharth Jayaprakash, “The Northern Sea Route and the Changing Geopolitics of the Russian Arctic,” ORF Occasional Paper No. 584, Observer Research Foundation, November 2026.

The Arctic is a late entrant into global geostrategic and geoeconomic discourse. In the past, thick ice and a lack of technological progress limited navigation in the region, restricting voyages to short distances during the summer and autumn months. However, a thawing Arctic due to climate change, combined with technological advancements, has increased the prospects of opening the region to year-round navigation.

Three prominent sea routes connect the Arctic to the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. The first is the Northwest Passage that runs along the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. The second is the Transpolar Sea Route, which passes through the North Pole. Finally, the Northeast Passage, referred to as the Northern Sea Route (NSR) in popular parlance, is a prominent, semi-enclosed coastal route along Russia’s Northern Coast with a wide continental shelf spanning from the ice-free port of Murmansk in the northwest through the Barents Sea, Kara Sea, Laptev Sea, East Siberian Sea, and Chukchi Sea to the Bay of Provideniya (see Map 1). The route can be further extended eastwards to Vladivostok and westwards to St Petersburg.

The Arctic region is of considerable importance for Moscow and is deeply embedded in its national consciousness.[1] Its primacy in domestic policy began in the twentieth century, when the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics’ (USSR) contestation with the United States (US) led to an increase in threat perceptions in the region.[2] In the current century, Russia’s Arctic policy focuses on securing its economic future through massive energy resource extraction and developing the NSR.[3] The Russian Arctic is laden with an estimated 35,700 billion cubic metres of gas and 2,300 million metric tonnes of oil, as well as huge reserves of minerals.[4] Apart from resource exploitation, Moscow wants to develop the Arctic regions and the maritime infrastructure along its coastline to make maritime shipping commercially viable. Achieving these objectives will require substantial capital and investment, for which Moscow has looked abroad for investors.
In this context, the NSR is the fulcrum of Russia’s Arctic strategy and is perceived

as a critical maritime artery for Moscow. The thawing of the Arctic has resulted in the route being identified as a potential international transport corridor, connecting the region to Europe and the rapidly growing Asian economies, thus complementing Russia’s strategy of turning to the East.[5] Since the 2010s, foreign firms have expressed interest in utilising the NSR, a pull factor for the development of the route, given that it is devoid of important chokepoints. By the mid-2010s, Moscow unveiled key energy projects in the Yamal and Gyda Peninsulas, increasing the NSR’s geoeconomic impetus.[6]

Despite Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the subsequent onset of Western sanctions against it, most foreign firms, barring ExxonMobil, Shell, and notable oilfield services companies, continued to operate in the NSR and did not pull out their investments from Russian energy projects. Nonetheless, Russia’s relations with other Arctic Council countries began to deteriorate and were severed following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.[7]

With full-scale sanctions being imposed on Russia in 2022, Western firms began withdrawing from Russian Arctic projects, particularly those in the realms of energy, mineral extraction, and maritime infrastructure.[9] In the same year, the NSR recorded zero international transit voyages, meaning that no vessel travelled from a non-Russian port to a Russian port using this route.[10] These trends were indicative of a deceleration of international shipping in contrast to the previous decade.

Since the outbreak of the Russia–Ukraine war, two trends have emerged in the Russian Arctic. First, the diminishing impetus for international cooperation because of the Russia–West contestation has raised the threat perceptions in the region.[11] The expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), marked by Finland and Sweden joining the alliance, has resulted in the Arctic increasingly featuring in Russia’s national security discourse.[12] Second, Russia’s relations with China have further consolidated, particularly in the Arctic, marked by increasing security cooperation and Beijing gaining privileged access to the region.

This paper traces the evolution of Russia’s development of the NSR and charts its trajectory within the context of Russia’s Arctic strategy against the backdrop of the geopolitical shifts. It examines the evolving role of regional and extra-regional players—such as the US, China, and India—prompted by geopolitical shifts in the region.
Before the Russia–Ukraine conflict, the NSR’s development could be divided into three key phases: Cold-War-induced autarky, the precondition for take-off, and accelerated development.

This phase focuses on the NSR’s growth from the early twentieth century to the dissolution of the USSR. Despite records of transit from as early as the sixteenth century,[13] the NSR was formally institutionalised in 1932, with the establishment of the Main Directorate of the Northern Sea Route (Glavsevmorput).[14] Incidentally, in the same year, Soviet scientist Otto Schmidt successfully navigated the entire NSR in 65 days.[15] International cooperation during this phase was limited, except during the Second World War, when the Arctic ports of Murmansk and Arkhangelsk were used as critical routes for lend–lease supply[a] from the Allied countries (see Map 3).[16] However, the intensification of the Cold War, marked by deteriorating relations between the US and the USSR, placed the Arctic at the centre of their military competition and nuclear deterrence. The region became heavily politicised.[17] The route also received considerable attention as a critical inland waterway. Furthermore, thanks to technological advancements since the 1950s, navigation along the route improved considerably, reflected in the growing transit volumes. In 1987, cargo transit had crossed 6.5 million tonnes, the highest in the twentieth century.[18]

The late 1980s saw a shift in the discourse around the Arctic, marked by Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev’s landmark proposal to transform the Arctic Circle from a military theatre to a zone of peace.[19] This shifted the focus of Arctic diplomacy from security issues to critical non-traditional matters, such as scientific research and environmental protection. Analysts note that Gorbachev’s speech at Murmansk in 1987 was the precursor to the establishment of the Arctic Council in 1996.[20] The latter emerged as an important forum to address pressing Arctic concerns, such as climate change, fishing, sustainable development, and indigenous rights. In 1991, the NSR was opened to international trade;[21] however, for two decades, it developed at a slow pace, far from the Cold War freight volumes, due to a state of de-industrialisation, lack of government investment, and technological backwardness.

In the 1990s, Russia, along with other European and Asian countries, undertook transit voyages between Japanese and Scandinavian and Baltic ports via the NSR.[22] In 1997, it ratified the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS),[23] and in 2001 it submitted an application to expand its Arctic shelf.[24] The last event is considered the starting point of the Arctic Policy of the Russian Federation.[25]
Two important pieces of legislation were passed during this period:

• The 2008 Foundations of State Policy in the Russian Arctic outlined national security priorities and led to a return of long-range bomber patrols, which had been discontinued at the end of the Cold War.[26] It also outlined the pathway towards socioeconomic development.

• The 2012 Law on the Northern Sea Route attempted to regulate commercial navigation across the NSR.[27] As part of these efforts, a permit system was introduced for commercial vessels, mandating the use of icebreaker and pilotage services. There was a growing impetus from Moscow’s political elite to promote the NSR for international transit between Europe and Asia. This was reflected in a 2011 speech by then Prime Minister Vladimir Putin, which highlighted the profitability of the route as compared to the southern route via the Suez Canal.[28] Countries such as China, Japan, South Korea, and Singapore expressed interest in using the NSR, given the politically unstable climate in the Middle East in the 2000s.[29] Reduced transit time and increasing Russian attention to the development of the route resulted in an uptick in voyages—between 2010 and 2019, more than 89 international transit voyages (those not headed to a Russian port) were made via the NSR.[30]

The NSR’s development accelerated in the 2010s, with a marked increase in the volumes of cargo transported domestically and internationally (see Figure 1). This shift can be attributed to a rise in Russian exports of natural resources from the Arctic and directly correlated to the development of critical oil and gas projects, such as Yamal Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG), Novy Port, and Arctic LNG-2.[31] It led to a shift in state policy, with the number of voyages from Russian ports to European and Asian ones increasing. More than 68 such voyages were conducted between 2010 and 2019.[32] Despite the deterioration of Russia’s relations with the West after 2014, foreign participation in the NSR increased year on year. By 2017, in a span of two years, the volume of transit shipping doubled to 11 million tonnes (see Figure 1).

The following year, Moscow announced that it would scale up the volume of transit to 80 million tonnes by 2024.[33] Conversely, during this period, the Russia–West contestation led to the Arctic region becoming increasingly securitised, reflected in key documents such as the 2015 Maritime Doctrine of the Russian Federation, the 2017 Fundamentals of State Policy in the Field of Naval Activities, and the 2021 National Security Doctrine.[34],[35] These documents called for securing Russia’s Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ), the protection of territorial sovereignty, and perceived the activities of external actors in the region as a threat to Russia’s national security.[36] At the same time, Russian military exercises in the Arctic increased. Subsequently, Moscow revamped the military infrastructure across the Arctic region and re-operationalised several Cold War bases.[37]

The NSR’s regulation also became over-centralised. In 2017, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed an Act granting vessels sailing under the Russian flag the exclusive right to transport and store natural gas, oil, and other resources extracted in the region under Russian jurisdiction.[38] In 2018, the responsibilities of the Northern Sea Route Administration were transferred to the Russian state-owned nuclear energy company, Rosatom,[39] making it responsible for development, operational control, and expanding the existing icebreaker fleet. Additional laws were introduced, enabling only Russian-flagged vessels to seek icebreaker assistance and restricting the entry of foreign-built icebreakers,[40] under the rationale of bolstering the domestic shipbuilding industry and driving import substitution. Even though foreign firms were not directly impacted by these legislative changes, the NSR’s attractiveness was reduced,[41] with Western countries deliberating on using other northern routes, such as the transpolar route through the North Pole, given the thawing of the Arctic ice.[42] However, activity along the NSR grew, with a rise in the presence of non-Arctic Asian states such as China, Japan, and South Korea, whose participation in energy projects in the Russian Arctic increased.[43]

In the 2010s, energy transit remained the mainstay of Russia’s strategy for the NSR. The onshore and offshore resource profile of the Arctic region is vast—its recoverable oil and gas reserves account for 60 percent of all recoverable hydrocarbons in Russia.[46] There are 15 active and prospective investment projects in the Arctic,[47] 11 of which are related to oil and gas, including Yamal, the Arctic LNG projects, the Varandey oil field, Vankor oil, and Payakha. The other four are related to ore and coal mining (see Map 2). Even though deposits in the region were discovered and, to some extent, developed during the Cold War, the importance of these projects grew after the adoption of the Maritime Doctrine of the Russian Federation,[48] which recommended developing the NSR as a transport corridor for the export of Russian hydrocarbons.
Source: Parlamentskaya Gazeta.[49]

Even with a wide resource basket, extraction is not the sole challenge that Moscow has had to grapple with. A lot of factors are at play while considering commercial viability of the projects in the Russian Arctic.

The first challenge is to ensure year-round accessibility of the NSR, so that Russian energy and minerals can reach the Western and Asian markets through northern delivery. Second, shipping along the NSR falls under a niche category that is unsuitable for container shipping, as container ships rely on tighter schedules and require multiple port calls. However, the weather patterns of the high north lead to delays. Furthermore, neither the port infrastructure nor the supply chains have been configured to support container ships. At present, the NSR is more useful for bulk and tanker shipping.
The third challenge is connectivity. For the domestic supply chains to be more resilient, railways, roadways, inland waterways, and airport networks must be better linked with the NSR ports.

The final challenge is ensuring human development in the region through initiatives such as creating employment opportunities, incentivising labour migration into the area, and developing new towns and settlements.

The impetus to undertake these massive developmental efforts and make the NSR economically feasible is reflected in the Fundamentals of the Russian Federation State Policy in the Arctic for the Period up to 2035[50] and further elaborated in the Strategy for the Development of the Arctic Zone of the Russian Federation and Provision of National Security for the Period to 2035.[51]
The Policy calls for development of the Arctic region in three key phases:
• The first stage (2020–2024) calls for scaling up transit to 80 million tonnes,[52] constructing more icebreakers, and developing container shipping hubs.
• The second phase (2025–2030) seeks to attain year-round navigation along the entirety of the NSR.

• The final phase (2031–2035) envisages further scaling up of maritime infrastructure across the NSR and improving the route’s competitiveness by increasing tonnage to more than 200 million tonnes and commissioning more icebreakers.[53]

The NSR starts from the ice-free port of Murmansk on the Kola Peninsula, sailing eastwards. Vessels travelling on it are outfitted at Murmansk or Arkhangelsk and head east, calling at the ports of Dikson, Dudinka, Igarka, Nordvik, Tiksi, and Ambarchik near the Kolyma River. Their voyage ends at Pevek and Provideniya (see Map 3).

Russia maintains a fleet of icebreaking ships that ensure year-round access to the NSR. Moscow has the largest fleet, consisting of more than 40 ships.[54] As of 2025, Russia is the only country that operates nuclear-powered icebreakers. Currently, Rosatom’s subsidiary Atomflot operates eight nuclear-powered icebreakers,[55] with the larger aim of securing year-round navigation within this decade. Port logistics have also been given considerable attention. Most of the 70 transhipment bases along the NSR require considerable repairs and reconstruction, as well as dredging, to accommodate larger vessels. Improving shipbuilding capacity is another area the Russian government has prioritised. Several shipbuilding facilities have been constructed, among which the most prominent is the Zvezda shipbuilding complex.[56] Established in 2015, the complex has delivered 12 ships within a decade, with more than 23 vessels under construction and a backlog of 50 orders.[57]

Moscow has also focused on the development of inland river transportation networks,[58] including the Ob, Yenisei, Northern Dvina, Pechora, Kolyma, Yana, and Indigirka. Since 2023, Russia has attempted to ship coal via the Ob-Irtysh river basin and the Yenisei to the Arctic ports. These developments reflected the growing importance of the NSR in Russia’s discourse.

However, these developments occurred against the backdrop of Russia’s waning relations with other Arctic Council countries, and the resultant securitisation of the Arctic region. This led to suspension of meetings between the heads of the armed forces of Arctic Council states and Russia.[59] In 2020, a new law was introduced, requiring foreign warships entering the NSR to seek approval 90 days before passage.[60]

The increasing threat perceptions in the Arctic have led to countries such as the US bolstering their latent military capabilities, by, for instance, prioritising the construction of maritime infrastructure and icebreakers.[61] Additionally, NATO forces have enhanced their presence in the Arctic through increased military drills.[62] These attempts to militarise the region, alongside the Great Power competition to gain regional influence, have put Arctic exceptionalism[b] on the backburner.

Russia’s war in Ukraine was a watershed moment for the Arctic region. While the Arctic was not directly impacted by the war, this was the first conflict of such magnitude in Europe since the end of the Second World War. It raised alarm bells in Europe and led to a rise in threat perception.

Since February 2022, three structural shifts have taken place. First, the institutional mechanisms responsible for Arctic governance were impacted by the war. The Arctic Council unequivocally condemned the Russian invasion of Ukraine and suspended cooperation with Russia.[63] In response, Moscow withdrew from the Barents Euro-Arctic Council.[c],[64] Second, the absence of governance mechanisms in the region has minimised cooperation in non-traditional areas, such as scientific research, economics, and trade. Third, Russia’s isolation from the West and the sanctions imposed on it led to transit along the NSR shifting eastwards towards China.

In the security realm, a palpable shift took place in the regional balance of power after Finland and Sweden were granted NATO membership.[65] NATO countries also began bolstering their military readiness since the invasion. The United Kingdom (UK) and France outlined their Arctic strategies and the Nordic countries ramped up their military spending. NATO members conducted multiple exercises in the Arctic, such as Cold Response 2022, Immediate Response 2024, Nordic Response 2024, Ice Camp 2024, and Arctic Edge.[66] The US updated its National Strategy for the Arctic Region first in 2022 and again in 2024, calling for enhanced presence in domain awareness, and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), as well as strengthened engagement with partners to uphold deterrence and defence.[67] Since the 2020s, military bases and installations in Greenland and Alaska have been revamped.

Moscow has viewed these developments with caution.[68] Doctrinally, Russia’s military responses in the Arctic have not radically changed, but it has strengthened the security aspect of its Arctic strategy, reflected in the developments since the war. For instance, in 2024, a decision was taken to integrate the Northwestern Arctic regions into the Leningrad military district, citing operational efficiency.[69] In the same year President Putin ordered the establishment of the Maritime Collegium headed by former Secretary of the Russian National Security Council Nikolai Patrushev.[70] The Collegium’s tasks include bolstering Russia’s defence and security in the world’s oceans, developing the NSR as a national transportation hub with linkages to global shipping routes, and enhancing the environmental protection.

Since the outbreak of the war, the Western terminating node, the Barents Sea, has witnessed rising threat perceptions. The attacks on the Russian–European Nord Stream Pipeline;[71] the alleged destruction of undersea infrastructure by Russian and Chinese ships;[72] and Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia’s long-range aviation assets, airfields, and energy infrastructure in Northern regions such as Murmansk[73] have exposed the Arctic to security threats. These shifts have heavily impacted the NSR.

Furthermore, the withdrawal of participation of European, American, Japanese, and South Korean shipping firms from the Arctic energy projects has marginalised the region’s geoeconomic importance. This includes most of the investments from Western companies and sudden withdrawal from firms such as the Norwegian Equinor, French Total and Schlumberger, and the American ExxonMobil (complete withdrawal).[74] The withdrawal resulted in a political-economic rejig in the Arctic region, with increased state control. The lack of foreign investment in the region, not to mention the absence of Western oil and gas field service providers and shipbuilding firms, has created additional strain on Russia, requiring it to domestically manufacture the technologies required for mineral extraction and shipbuilding at exorbitant costs.

Furthermore, the number of voyages across the NSR reduced. From 2016–19, of the 1,232 foreign voyages made along the NSR, 1,108 voyages were made from and to Europe, while 124 voyages were made from Europe to Asia. From 2023 onwards, most of the foreign ships operating along the NSR were Chinese. Interestingly, even with international cooperation along the NSR remaining limited during the war—apart from the increased presence of Chinese firms—the United Arab Emirates’ DP World signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Rosatom to develop container shipment transit along the NSR.[75] This reflected a growing interest from Asian countries to engage with Russia in the Arctic.

Apart from enhancing trade with Asia, Moscow’s Arctic strategy since the Ukraine invasion has evolved to give a stronger impetus to domestic infrastructure development goals and capacity-building. This is seen in the 2022 Russian Arctic Strategy to 2035,[76] an exhaustive developmental plan for the NSR that outlines projects with target years for completion. These include the construction of additional nuclear-powered icebreakers, port development and shipbuilding projects, construction of LNG and coal terminals, expansion of railway infrastructure in the Arctic region, and development of space technologies (including monitoring, hydrometeorological, and hydrographic support systems, as well as remote sensing capabilities). Additionally, the Strategy estimates the trajectory of tonnage from various Arctic projects and envisages that by 2035, the total tonnage along the NSR will increase to 238 million tonnes. However, so far, the targets mentioned in it have not been attained. For instance, the 2018 benchmark of reaching 80 million tonnes was not achieved as of 2025; the volume transported via the NSR instead reduced by 2.3 percent compared to 2024, remaining at 37 million tonnes.[77]

Going by the current level of hostility between Russia and Ukraine and the heightened mistrust between Russia and the West, it is unlikely that Moscow’s relations with the West will return to pre-war levels in the near future. Given the EU’s commitment to phase out its future hydrocarbon imports from Russia by 2027,[78] its energy demand will decrease, forcing Russia to find new markets to export its oil and gas.

Since 2022, trade flows along the NSR have been increasingly rerouted eastwards. If the EU reneges on the purchase of Russian energy, the energy value chains would have to pivot the same way. In this context, the NSR would not be commercially viable, as the distance to Asian markets is farther than to European markets. Additionally, the markets in Asia cannot match the volumes of oil and gas exported to Europe. Lastly, if international sanctions continue, Russia will have to grapple with limitations in accessing critical technology and oilfield services, which will lead to growing dependence on China.

Russian–Chinese relations have improved due to Russia’s contestation with the West, reflected in the discourse surrounding the NSR. The Chinese engagement with the route can be traced back 2011, when a tanker loaded with gas condensate left the Purovsky gas processing plant in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug in Russia for the port of Ningbo in China.[79] In 2013, Beijing was granted observer status in the Arctic Council, giving it a higher status.[80]

China’s articulation of strengthening connectivity across Eurasia and the Arctic is formally prescribed in its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). Russia was initially sceptical of the growing Chinese footprint in Eurasia and did not subscribe to the BRI, as Beijing’s flagship Eurasian geoeconomic project would undermine the Russia-backed Eurasian Economic Union’s (EAEU) efforts, which aim to strengthen economic integration in the region. However, perceptions changed later, with Moscow viewing it as an opportunity to enhance connectivity across Eurasia. In the summer of 2015, the EAEU was formally linked with the BRI. In the same year, then Deputy Prime Minister of Russia Dmitry Rogozin invited Beijing to participate and invest in joint infrastructure projects along the NSR.[81]

In 2018, China launched the Polar Silk Road (PSR),[82] also dubbed the ‘global waterway’ in Chinese, as an extension of the BRI, to connect its northeastern ports in Asia to Northern European ports via the Arctic (see Map 4). The PSR traverses through the Northeast passage, the Northwest passage, and the Central passage, and is perceived as an alternative to the Maritime Silk Road that contains prominent chokepoints such as the Strait of Malacca and the Bab el-Mandeb. The PSR has chokepoints along the way as well, such as the Bering Strait, but scholars argue that during certain seasons, using this route is more cost-effective, even with the employment of icebreakers.[83] More importantly, being the largest exporter and second-largest importer of goods, China needs this route as an important alternative to minimise the risk of supply-chain disruptions and blockades, which would result in commodity goods’ prices rising. China’s growing fleet of icebreaker vessels and its exploratory voyages also reflect this concern.

Since the Russia–Ukraine war, Chinese companies have started replacing Western and Northeast Asian firms in the Arctic region, leading to an increase in Russia–China bilateral trade. Beijing has now become Russia’s largest trading partner instead of the EU, mainly due to hydrocarbon exports being rerouted to China, and Chinese goods and technology flooding the Russian market. Beijing has also been receiving LNG and oil from Arctic ports.

Since the mid-2010s, China has been increasingly importing Russian energy over land through the Power of Siberia gas pipeline and the Eastern Siberia–Pacific Ocean (ESPO) oil pipeline, and via the high seas along the Southern routes and NSR. This has led prominent Russian oil and gas firms to conclude contracts with Chinese companies. In 2018, the Russian Vnesheconombank (VEB) signed a deal with the China Development Bank (CDB) to jointly develop projects in the NSR. The China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) and the Silk Road Fund jointly own a 29.9 percent stake in the Yamal LNG project.[84] In 2019, Beijing officially entered the Arctic LNG-2 project by acquiring a 10 percent stake in the project, and China National Chemical Engineering Group and Neftegazholding signed a deal to develop the Payakha oilfield in Russia. Beijing has expressed interest in connecting the Sabetta port in Russia with the Eurasian Rail network as part of the Northern Latitudinal Railway, which would extend the railway line to Bovanenkovo gas field on the Yamal Peninsula.

Since the Russia–Ukraine war, China has gained privileged access to the Russian Arctic, with 95 percent of foreign transit along the NSR taking place between Russia and China.[85] Beijing has expressed interest in investing in important ports along the NSR, such as Murmansk and Arkhangelsk. The Chinese firm NewNew Shipping Line Co. has agreed to invest US$2.5 billion to support the construction of new port facilities in Arkhangelsk,[86] while the China Poly Group and the China Ocean Shipping Company (COSCO) have expressed interest in using the NSR for container shipping to the port as well.

In 2024, Rosatom partnered with NewNew Shipping Co. Limited to establish year-round shipping along the NSR.[87] Ninety-two voyages carrying more than 3 million tonnes of cargo were made along the NSR that year. In September 2025, China launched its first container-shipping route to Europe via the NSR, connecting to European ports such as Felixstowe, Rotterdam, Hamburg, and Gdańsk.[88]

No heavy investments have been made under the BRI or PSR in Russia. Developments following the Russia–Ukraine war have led to certain complications in Chinese engagements in the Arctic, while there is an increasing appetite for investing in the Arctic and converging interests. An assessment of Chinese engagement in the region is indicative of Beijing being cognisant of secondary sanctions, which have limited its engagement under the BRI-PSR framework. In other words, while China’s presence may be improving, as reflected in increasing voyages and investing in certain port facilities, there is no large-scale Chinese investment in the Arctic.

Since the 2010s Russia and China have participated in joint aviation patrols and strategic bomber overflights over the Sea of Japan and the East China Sea in proximity to the Japanese and South Korean Air Defence Identification Zones (ADIZ).[89] Both countries have scaled up their patrols in the North Pacific region since 2021, as well as near the Aleutian Islands, close to the American EEZ.[90] Since the war, the cooperation in the security sphere has continued to increase between them. The Russian Federal Security Service Border Service and the Chinese Coast Guard signed an MoU in 2023 to bolster soft security cooperation to combat terrorism, illegal migration, and provide joint humanitarian assistance and conduct disaster relief operations.[91] Both countries completed their first strategic bomber patrol along the Alaskan ADIZ without violating the US airspace. In the following year, Russian and Chinese coast guard vessels jointly patrolled the Arctic and held maritime drills.

Western experts have highlighted that this strategic convergence led to the disruption of critical undersea infrastructure in the Baltic Sea region in 2023 and 2024. Russian and Chinese vessels allegedly damaged several undersea cables, including the Balticconnector gas pipeline. In 2024, it was reported that Russian vessels damaged the Estlink powerlines between Finland and Estonia. Experts opine that this cooperation in undersea warfare could be replicated in the Arctic theatre. Even with the discourse around the war in Ukraine shifting after the Republican Party administration took a conciliatory position vis-à-vis Moscow, Russia–China relations have not seen a deceleration.

In August 2025, both countries concluded a 15-day joint maritime patrol in the Western Pacific.[92] Russian experts feel that the converging security interests between the two countries have been driven by the collective West’s aims to stymie China’s peaceful rise and counterbalance Russia through initiatives such as the Quad and AUKUS (Australia–UK–US). Despite China’s growing footprint in the NSR, the possibility of both nations veering towards an alliance remains remote, as the partnership seems indicative rather than institutional. Additionally, Moscow is concerned about the growing asymmetry in its relations with Beijing.[93]

With the Russia–China relationship consolidating in the Arctic, US policy began to take a turn to stall this. US President Donald Trump has maintained a conciliatory position towards Russia’s security interests.[94] In the first conversations between American and Russian negotiating parties, cooperation in the Arctic was raised. Washington expressed its interest in investing in energy projects as well as cooperating on environmental issues.[95]

The impact of the initial talks could be observed in Putin’s speech at the Sixth International Arctic Forum in Murmansk in March 2025, where he announced that he welcomed investments from foreign countries, including Western ones, in the Arctic.[96] This was a change in tone as compared to the last three years. Later, the Putin–Trump summit in Alaska in August 2025 marked a new turn in the bilateral relationship as days after the visit, Putin signed a decree enabling Western firms to recoup their losses following the Russian government’s decision to nationalise the Sakhalin-1 oil project in 2022.[97] These developments resulted in US allies such as South Korea expressing interest in re-engaging in the Russian Arctic. In August 2026, a South Korean ship sailed from Busan to Felixstowe in the UK, saving up to 10 days one way.[98]

There are three plausible explanations for a Russia–US convergence on Arctic issues. First, a potential revival of energy projects in the region while simultaneously curbing China’s growing presence. Second, the US wants to strengthen its critical mineral supply chains by tapping into deposits located in Russia’s northern territories. Third, improved ties could help the US offset its infrastructural shortcomings in the Arctic, particularly the underdevelopment of ports and the limited availability of icebreaking vessels, effectively buying time to build capacity.

Some experts argue that scaling up cooperation between the two countries in the Arctic could result in Russia granting greater agency to Washington in its interest in expanding its presence in Greenland,[99] although Russia’s position on the Greenland issue—wherein it expresses concern with the expanding US alliance with the latter—has not changed. Additionally, given the lack of strategic convergence, and the unpredictability of US foreign policy under Trump, it is too soon to ascertain the future of Russia–US cooperation.

Russia’s deteriorating ties with the Arctic Council countries has stalled cooperation on Arctic governance. Subsequently, it has called for the participation of Asian countries, such as India and China, in the Arctic. In Moscow’s calculus, the Easternisation of the Arctic by the introduction of new players would partially offset the West, and for Asian states, this would translate to a foothold in the region.
In this context, with its historical ties with the Arctic from as early as 1920, when it signed the Svalbard Treaty,[100] India can emerge as an important player in the Arctic.

New Delhi’s presence, though, is not significant currently; it started operating an Arctic outpost in Svalbard in 2008. In 2013, along with China, Japan, South Korea, and Singapore, India was granted observer status in the Arctic Council. This signalled a positive development for the Arctic and the non-Arctic states.[101]
India’s Arctic policy lies within the pillars of enhancing cooperation in science and technology, economic and human development, climate change, Arctic governance, and enhancing connectivity.

Since the late 2010s, India’s perception of the Arctic has begun to shift from being dominated in the realm of science to being receptive to engaging along new pillars; this is because of the strengthening geoeconomic discourse in the Arctic, particularly the prospects of reduced transit time along the NSR, and new avenues for energy imports. Additionally, the growing presence of China in the NSR and its gaining privileged access to investing in the Arctic region has seen a growing impetus to enhance Indian engagement in the Arctic.

The engagement is additionally driven by the prospect of keeping India’s relations with Russia strong by finding new means to strengthen cooperation. The culmination of these interests was reflected in the 2019 Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok where New Delhi accepted Moscow’s invitation to invest in Russian Arctic projects.[102] India has further committed to investing in infrastructure development in the NSR and plans to scale up the use of the northern route in the future for the import of Russian hydrocarbons. Before 2019, India had investments in energy projects in the sub-Arctic and Arctic region, such as ONGC’s Sakhalin-1, and in Vankor field (140 km from Igarka).

Moreover, New Delhi’s interests in the NSR emerge from the idea of extending the Eastern Maritime Corridor, linking it with the Eastern Indian ports, enabling circular connectivity with Russia along three directions—the existing route via Mumbai to St Petersburg, the route via the Caucasus using the International North South Transport Corridor, and third, the Eastern Maritime Corridor. The NSR will complement these routes, enhancing connectivity between the Russian Arctic and Indian ports.

The interest in enhancing engagement along the NSR was reflected in the visit of Russian Minister for the Development of the Far East and the Arctic Alexei Chekunkov to New Delhi to discuss the transportation of goods through the NSR.[103] The Arctic and the NSR have emerged as important discussion points in the India–Russia relationship, reflected in their joint statements since the 2010s. In 2024, both sides set up a working group on the NSR.[104] Apart from the discussion on commencing cargo transit target, New Delhi is interested in participating in joint projects in Arctic shipbuilding, which will further improve India’s domestic shipbuilding capabilities. Additionally, India is interested in signing agreements that would enable Indian seafarers to gain training from Russia in polar navigation. There is a growing need for shipbuilding infrastructure for the NSR, for which Moscow has begun outsourcing the building of non-nuclear icebreakers to third countries. Against this backdrop, India is in talks with Russia to build four non-nuclear icebreakers.[105]

However, despite the growing interests and the formation of an institutional framework to strengthen cooperation in the NSR, Indian investments in the Arctic have been minimal. Moreover, the threat of sanctions has influenced India’s engagement. For example, in 2024, India’s oil secretary announced that New Delhi would not import LNG from the sanctioned Arctic LNG-2 project.[106] Second, the route to North America from India via the NSR at present remains commercially unviable. Apart from the requirement of ice-class vessels, it would be a challenge to ensure the safety of cargoes traversing along the NSR. Additionally, the NSRs are more suitable for the transit of bulk cargo than container shipping, which complicates transit. Lastly, given the lack of comparative advantages India has in its export basket, the NSR’s feasibility reduces. Notwithstanding these challenges, India notes the viability of the route due to the thawing of the ice, which comes with the opportunity of participating in joint projects, building equity early on. These factors can be attributed to India’s core interests in the NSR.

Apart from the sanctions imposed on it, Russia’s waning relations with the West have reduced the economic impetus for Western businesses and governments to invest in projects along the NSR. According to Russia’s strategy for the development of the NSR (see Table 1), cargo volumes should have reached 110 million tonnes; however, they have reduced instead, showing how the war in Ukraine and subsequent developments were a critical variable in shaping the NSR’s development.
Second, from a geoeconomic lens, there are eight factors that influence the attractiveness of a transport route:
• Cost of delivery
• Route reliability
• Delivery time
• Requirements and flexibility
• Infrastructure
• Crew experience
• Sanctions regulation
• Customs clearance

The NSR ranks highly in terms of the distance covered; however, there are additional costs that a shipping company would have to bear, such as hiring an icebreaker. The reliability of the route is also questionable, given the adverse climatic conditions (low temperatures, dense fog, and other such factors).

The NSR has waterways and shallow reefs, with the water depth being as low as 8 metres in certain areas in the Chukchi Sea and the East Siberian Sea, and an average depth of 50 metres, which makes it unsuitable for container shipping. Additionally, in certain parts, such as from the Bering Strait to Murmansk (4,000 km), there are no ports with facilities.

The cost of constructing ice-class vessels is also 30 percent higher than that of a regular ship. Furthermore, the infrastructure facilities in the ports have to match shipping company requirements—even though there are sufficient ports in the Arctic, most of them are not equipped with modern facilities. There are also geoeconomic impediments such as high insurance premiums and the threat of secondary sanctions.

Domestically, the Russian government’s ambitious efforts to scale up economic activity in the Russian north will require a fair amount of capital. The growing contestation with the West has led to a lack of access to Western critical technologies and software, which means that the Russian government will have to deal with the transaction costs of sourcing technologies from other countries such as China and engaging in import substitution projects where Russia has no comparative advantage. In other words, developing the northern regions is expensive and requires massive capital investment from the West; Chinese support by itself will not suffice. Vessels sailing along the NSR also require more skilled crew members, given the lack of expertise in polar navigation.

Finally, despite environmental protection featuring in the NSR discourse, the rising economic activity along the route has resulted in increasing emissions and air and water pollution. The accelerated melting of ice and rising sea levels threaten the Arctic ecosystem and biodiversity.

Russia has a first-mover advantage in the Arctic; the vast coastline within its borders has promoted the development of its maritime infrastructure, which has put it ahead of other Arctic players such as the US or Canada. Its strategy for the NSR’s further development is driven by the prospect of the Arctic’s thawing. Its early efforts in rebuilding Arctic ports and scaling up shipbuilding have had multiplier effects, resulting in the creation of employment opportunities across regions and development of new cities across the NSR, setting up the long-term growth of the corridor.

The return of Russia to the global markets, if sanctions are lifted, and with longer ice-free months due to global warming as well as the construction of a vast icebreaker fleet with the help of foreign partners, can result in the NSR becoming a viable transit corridor. However, the route’s usage will be contingent on global economic conditions and other demand-and-supply factors that govern the operations of all international transport corridors. Given the current state of Arctic shipping, the volume of cargo is likely to increase; however, the scramble for Arctic routes as portrayed in popular discourse will not persist, which means that the growth of the route in the following decades is likely to be linear. Concerns still prevail, such as higher operational costs, the difficulty of gaining financing, and the limited export/import basket, which makes the NSR’s development challenging. That said, Moscow views the NSR as an opportunity—it is the most viable Northern route and adjacent to the coastline, with swathes of mineral and hydrocarbon reserves. Cognisant of its future validity, both as an international transit and energy corridor, Russia is incrementally building capacity in its northern regions, preparing for the prospect of an ice-free future.
